articles.title: Melinjo (L.) seed extract for treatment of sleep/wake fragmentation in diet-induced obese mice
articles.full_text:
Introduction

Recent scientific and media reports have highlighted increased interest in sleep apnea syndrome, emphasizing the link between obesity and sleep disorders []. Epidemiological studies show a U-shaped relationship between obesity and total sleep duration, with individuals sleeping 6–7 h exhibiting the lowest obesity rates []. Both longer and shorter lengths of sleep correlate positively with higher obesity levels. Moreover, patients with obesity often experience more frequent
nocturnal awakenings and difficulty returning to sleep, leading to impaired sleep stability, which is exacerbated by concomitant sleep apnea syndrome [].
Given the challenges in determining the complex effects of obesity on sleep disorders and the underlying mechanisms through epidemiological studies alone, experimental obesity models have thus
been extensively investigated using laboratory animals, such as mice and rats, which share fundamental sleep architecture with humans, such as rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM)
sleep. Research on diet-induced obesity in mice following a high-fat diet (HFD) [] and genetically obese mice models, such as[] and[], has demonstrated higher sleep fragmentation, characterized by more frequent
awakenings and decreased mean length of sleep episodes.

To achieve a longer healthy life expectancy, diet-related obesity must be addressed, which will subsequently reduce the risk of lifestyle-related diseases and improve sleep stability.
Improved sleep stability supports the maintenance of physical, mental health, and cognitive functions, including memory []. The key to achieving these
objectives is integrating improvements in dietary habits, exercise routines, and lifestyle. However, because of difficulties in consistently implementing them in daily life, the effective use
of functional foods is encouraged. Melinjo (L.) seed extract (MSE) is one such anti-obesity functional food that can potentially stimulate energy metabolism. The
melinjo tree originates from Indonesia and is often called the “tree of life.” Its seeds are abundant in resveratrol, a type of polyphenol, including trans-resveratrol, gnetin C, gnemonoside
A, and gnemonoside D. Known for its caloric restriction-mimicking properties, trans-resveratrol may be responsible for the beneficial effects of MSE on metabolic processes [,]. The phenomenon known as the “French Paradox,” which refers to the observation that French nationals who, despite
having a diet rich in saturated fats, are predominantly healthy with long life expectancies, which has been attributed to their preference for red wine, which is rich in resveratrol. This
epidemiological paradox has led to an increased societal interest in the impact of resveratrol [].

MSE has tested negative for long-term toxicity [], which has earned it much research attention as a functional food ingredient. Moreover, its high
therapeutic efficacy has been proven in humans and mice for various conditions, including dementia [], cancer [] [], skin aging [], periodontal disease [], and the
reduction of serum uric acid levels []. We previously reported that MSE consumption by diet-induced obese mice increased energy expenditure through the
activation of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), a protein that facilitates heat production in brown adipose tissue, thereby ameliorating the conditions of obesity, fatty liver, and insulin
resistance while concurrently normalizing blood glucose levels []. A study revealed that MSE dietary supplementation in obese mice not only decreased
adiposity but also enhanced the overall glucose regulation and increased the survival rates []; however, no studies have reported about sleep
architecture. In the present study, we evaluated the influence of dietary MSE on sleep architecture in HFD-induced obese mice through a comprehensive assessment of sleep architecture using
frequency analysis focusing on the duration of sleep/wake episodes, incidence of brief awakenings (indicating light sleep), and the distribution of cortical activity during NREM sleep.

Materials and Methods

Animals

Three-week-old male C57BL/6J mice (CLEA Japan, Inc., Hamamatsu, Japan) with homogeneous average body weights were individually placed in plastic cages and housed in an air-conditioned
animal facility at 22 ± 2°C with a 12-h light–dark cycle (lights on 06:00–18:00). The animal experiment protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Tokai University
(Isehara, Japan). The minimization of the number of animals analyzed and that of any pain or discomfort were prioritized.

Following a week-long acclimatization period, the mice were divided into groups, which were subjected to one of four dietary conditions: 1) normal diet (ND) group (n=14) fed with CE-2
rodent diet (comprising 4.8 wt% fat, 25.1 wt% protein, 4.2 wt% fiber, and providing 361.2 kcal/100 g; CLEA Japan, Inc.); 2) HFD group (n=15) fed with HFD-32 (with 31.9 wt% fat [24.5 wt%
unsaturated fatty acids and 7.1 wt% saturated compounds], 25.5 wt% protein, 2.9 wt% fiber, and providing 507.6 kcal/100 g; CLEA Japan, Inc.); 3) ND+MSE group (n=11); and 4) HFD+MSE group
(n=13). Lyophilized MSE powder, composed of 0.1% trans-resveratrol, 1.6% gnetin C, 18.7% gnemonoside A, 3.8% gnemonoside D, and 9.0% dextrin was provided by Yamada Bee Co., Inc. (Okayama,
Japan), was prepared as described previously []. The MSE powder content was standardized to contain >20.0% resveratrol derivatives. The
MSE-supplemented diets were supplemented with 1% w/w lyophilized MSE powder. The body weights of the mice were assessed every Monday and Friday. After 16 weeks, the mice were then subjected
to sleep measurement studies.

Food intake measurement

Food intake was assessed at week 15. The weight of the food provided for 1 week was premeasured. After 1 week, the remaining food, bedding, feces, etc., were segregated by thoroughly
sieving the bedding in the cages, and the weight of the remaining food was calculated. The difference between the weight of the rationed and remaining food provided was divided by seven to
determine the daily food intake.

Surgery and polygraphic recordings

Electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) electrodes for recording polysomnographic parameters of sleep and wakefulness were embedded in the mice. Briefly, anesthesia was
performed in an induction chamber with 4% isoflurane (DS Pharma Animal Health Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan) dissolved in oxygen at 1.0 l/min. The animals were then removed and placed on a
stereotaxic frame with continuous mask anesthesia achieved with 2% isoflurane. The skull was exposed, and bones were washed with 10% hydrogen peroxide solution. Two stainless-steel screws
(diameter, 1.0 mm; Neuroscience, Tokyo, Japan) were positioned on the skull in the projection of the left cerebral hemisphere (frontal: 1.5 mm lateral to the midline, 1.0 mm anterior to the
bregma; parietal: 1.5 mm lateral to the midline, 1.0 mm anterior to the lambda) as per the Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates guidelines []. A
third screw was inserted over a frontal bone to serve as the ground electrode. EMG activity was controlled using stainless-steel Teflon-coated Cooner wires (Cooner Wire, Inc., Chatsworth,
CA, USA) placed bilaterally in the neck muscles. All electrodes were linked to a micro-connector, and the whole assembly was fixed to the skull with dental cement. Indomethacin (1 mg/kg,
i.p., Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Corp., Osaka, Japan) and penicillin G (800 U/kg, i.m., Meiji Seika Pharma Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) injections were performed prior to electrode placement.
All the manipulations were performed on a heating pad. The animals were allowed to recover for 10–14 days before transferring them to recording chambers for sleep studies.

Each mouse was placed in a plastic cage (300 × 210 × 210 mm) in an isolated and soundproof recording chamber (illumination intensity, 100 lx). EEG, EMG, and spontaneous locomotor activity
were evaluated for 24 h starting with the light cycle. The transferring cables were linked to a swivel contact, enabling the mice to move freely without limitations. Unihemispheric,
frontal-parietal EEG and neck EMG signals were recorded on a BAS-8201 polygraph (Biotex, Kyoto, Japan). The signals were amplified, underwent filtration (EEG, 0.5–30 Hz; EMG, 16–128 Hz),
digitization at 128 Hz, and were saved in 10-s epochs on a personal computer using the Vital Recorder software (Kissei Comtec, Nagano, Japan). Spontaneous homecage locomotor activity was
monitored via an infrared sensor (Biotex, Kyoto, Japan) positioned on the cage top. The values for the parameter were intensified and then transformed in a digital form at a sampling rate of
128 Hz for further recording using the Vital Recorder software.

Vigilance state determination and spectral analysis of the EEG

Polysomnographic records were automatically analyzed and scored offline for wakefulness and REM and NREM sleep in 10-s epochs, as per the standard guidelines for SleepSign ver.3 software
(Kissei Comtec, Nagano, Japan) []. All vigilance state classifications assigned by SleepSign version 3 were examined visually and corrected if
necessary. Spectral quantification of the EEG recorded during NREM sleep was performed using fast Fourier transformation (sampled at 128 Hz) with a power spectral profile over a range of
0–20 Hz divided into 1-Hz resolutions. The EEG power density in each frequency bin was normalized by the total power averaged from all epochs that were scored as NREM sleep throughout the
24-h period across all frequency bins. The relative delta power was calculated as the quotient of absolute NREM delta power (0–4 Hz) to the total EEG power.

Statistical analyses

The descriptive statistics for the data are expressed as mean ± SEM. One-way analysis of variance was performed, followed by the Scheffe’s post hoc test, to determine the associations
between the parameters among the groups with different experimental characteristics.

Results

Impact of MSE on body weight, food intake, and spontaneous locomotor activity

shows the changes in the body weights of mice over a 16-week period. The ND group exhibited a steady increase in the values of this parameter, which stabilized at approximately 28.0
g, whereas the HFD group showed a significant increase after week 8, reaching 40.9 g by the end of the experiment. Both the ND+MSE and HFD+MSE groups showed weight patterns similar to that
of the ND group. The outcomes demonstrated the protective effect of dietary MSE against HFD-induced obesity.demonstrates the increase in
the body weight of mice at the end of the experiment. The HFD group showed a 196% increase compared with the ND group. The ND+MSE and HFD+MSE groups showed weight gain patterns comparable to
those of the ND group. Despite this lipid-metabolizing effect of MSE, no significant difference in food intake and spontaneous locomotor activity were found between the four groups ().

Effect of MSE on sleep/wakefulness parameters

The impact of MSE on sleep/wakefulness parameters are described in. The mean daily amount of NREM sleep, REM sleep, and wakefulness did
not differ significantly between the four groups, indicating that neither HFD feeding nor MSE supplementation affected these values. Compared with the ND group, the average episode length of
NREM sleep significantly decreased by 63%, and the number of episodes rose by 159% in the HFD group, indicating NREM sleep fragmentation in HFD-induced obesity mice. The average duration and
the number of NREM sleep episodes in both the ND+MSE and HFD+MSE groups were comparable to those observed in the ND group. Compared with the ND group, the HFD group experienced a 65%
decrease in the average episode duration of wakefulness and a 158% increase in the number of episodes, indicating fragmentation of wakefulness. The average duration and number of wakefulness
episodes in both the ND+MSE and HFD+MSE groups were comparable to those observed in the ND group. These outcomes reveal the protective effect of dietary MSE against the fragmentation of NREM
sleep and wakefulness demonstrated in HFD-induced obesity mice. In contrast, no significant changes in REM sleep parameters were observed.

Effect of MSE on the length of NREM sleep, REM sleep, and wakefulness episodes

shows a histogram of the duration of NREM sleep episodes. The lengths of all NREM sleep episodes occurring within a 24-h period was categorized into the following intervals: 10, 20,
30–40, 50–80, 90–160, 170–320, 330–640, 650–1,280, and over 1,290 s. This classification facilitated the investigation of NREM sleep, where the frequency of episode lengths was most
affected. Compared with the ND group, the frequency of short NREM sleep episodes in the HFD group, the durations of which ranged from 20 to 160 s, increased significantly, whereas the
frequency of long NREM sleep episodes, which fluctuated from 330 to 640 s, significantly decreased. In the ND+MSE group, the occurrence of any NREM sleep episode duration was comparable to
that of the ND group, indicating no significant effect of MSE addition in the ND group. Conversely, the HFD+MSE group showed a reduced frequency of short NREM sleep duration, ranging from 20
to 40 s, comparable to that of the ND group but significantly lower than that of the HFD group. This indicates that MSE supplementation normalized the shortened NREM sleep episodes observed
in HFD-induced obesity mice.

presents a histogram of the duration of REM sleep episodes. Compared with the ND group, the frequency of short REM sleep episodes in the
HFD group, which ranged from 10 to 20 s, significantly increased. The duration of REM sleep episodes in the ND+MSE group was similar to that observed in the ND group, indicating that the
addition of MSE did not significantly affect the ND group. On the contrary, the HFD+MSE group exhibited a tendency toward a decrease in the frequency of short REM sleep episodes ranging from
10 to 20 s; however, this reduction did not achieve significance when compared with the HFD group.

presents a histogram of the duration of wakefulness episodes. In contrast with the ND group, the frequency of short wakefulness episodes,
ranging from 10 to 20 s, was significantly increased in the HFD group. The increase in brief awakenings of less than 20 s demonstrates the significant impact of dietary obesity. The
frequency of short wakefulness episodes was significantly lower in the HFD+MSE group than in the HFD group and comparable to that in the ND group. In the ND+MSE group, the incidence of any
wakefulness episode duration was similar to that in the ND group, indicating that MSE supplementation had no effect on a normal diet. Thus, MSE supplementation mitigated the brief awakenings
observed in HFD-caused obesity mice.

Effect of MSE on cortical EEG power

Cortical EEG power spectral () and delta power () analyses were performed to evaluate the effect of MSE supplementation on cortical activity during NREM sleep. The
power spectra of NREM sleep in the ND+MSE, HFD, and HFD+MSE groups were indistinguishable from that of the ND group, showing that neither HFD feeding nor MSE supplementation affected basal
cortical activity. Similarly, the delta power in the ND+MSE, HFD, and HFD+MSE groups were indistinguishable from that of the ND group, indicating that neither HFD feeding nor MSE
supplementation affected the depth or intensity of NREM sleep.

Discussion

Mice assigned an ND exhibited a high prevalence of sustained NREM sleep, whereas those under HFD experienced fragmentation of prolonged NREM sleep due to the occurrence of brief awakenings.
MSE supplementation in the HFD group suppressed this fragmentation, restoring the continuity of NREM sleep and improving overall sleep stability. Sleep stability may be diminished by the loss
of sleep continuity, similar to sleep fragmentation induced by mid-sleep awakenings in humans. Indeed, Tobler[] reported that
mice deficient in prion protein featured a significantly increased frequency of short awakenings compared with wild-type mice, indicating that the frequency of brief awakenings is an
informative index of sleep stability degradation promoted by the fragmentation of sleep–wake cycles. Therefore, the detrimental effect of HFD-induced obesity and the ameliorative influence of
MSE on sleep stability may be conveniently evaluated using the occurrence of brief awakenings as an indicator. Since evaluations based on the sustainability of NREM sleep in mice can be
extrapolated to humans with a similar sleep architecture, the potential benefit of MSE to humans is anticipated. In contrast, dietary supplementation with MSE had little effect in ND,
signifying no further enhancement of sleep stability beyond the normal state. During NREM sleep, excitatory inputs from the brainstem, hypothalamus, and basal forebrain to the cerebral cortex
and thalamus decrease, leading to synchronized neural activity in these regions and the predominance of low-frequency delta waves []. Delta activity on
EEG is recognized as a biomarker of homeostatic sleep drive and is frequently linked to both sleep duration and intensity []. Consequently, we examined
EEG power spectra and delta power during NREM sleep. Despite an increase in NREM sleep fragmentation in the HFD group, which was ameliorated by MSE supplementation, our findings revealed no
significant alterations in delta power due to either HFD feeding or MSE supplementation. Similarly, delta power remained unchanged by both HFD-induced weight gain and subsequent weight loss
[]. Given that delta power within a NREM sleep remains unaffected by brief awakenings or interruptions [],
it is plausible that delta power is resistant to changes induced by NREM sleep fragmentation under our experimental conditions.

Mice fed HFD for 19 weeks exhibited a two-fold increase in weight gain compared with their ND counterparts during the same period. However, in the HFD+MSE group, body weight was significantly
lower than that in the HFD group and comparable to that of the ND group. Yoneshiro[], who conducted a study under the same
experimental conditions as ours, performed biochemical evaluations and found that levels of blood glucose, serum free fatty acids, and insulin resistance index, which were increased in the HFD
group, were significantly reduced in the HFD+MSE group and comparable to those in the ND group. Thus, administering MSE at a 1% ratio in HFD effectively prevented the development of metabolic
syndrome caused by HFD-induced obesity. The mechanisms by which MSE ameliorates obesity and metabolic syndrome were then considered. While body weight is determined as the balance between
energy intake from diet and its expenditure from physical activity, such as exercise and daily living, negligible differences were observed in daily food intake and spontaneous physical
activity between the HFD and HFD+MSE groups (). Therefore, MSE may not have caused a reduction in food intake to induce a decrease energy
intake or elevate spontaneous physical activity accompanied by a higher energy expenditure. Yoneshiroalso performed Western blot analysis to evaluate the expression
levels of UCP1, which is a thermogenic protein localized primarily in brown adipose tissue and recognized as a thermogenic organ []. According to this
study, UCP1 expression in the HFD+MSE group was significantly higher than in the ND and HFD groups, implying that MSE enhances thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue by increasing UCP1
expression. UCP1, which is localized in the inner mitochondrial membrane, transforms energy into heat via uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation, thereby utilizing fat as an energy source.
Increased thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue may have induced a decrease in body fat, ultimately resulting in weight loss. On the contrary, body weight did not decrease in the ND+MSE group,
compared with that in the ND group. In humans, a higher activity of brown adipose tissue is associated with a lower accumulation of visceral fat, which progresses with age. Specifically, its
continuous exposure to cold stimuli for 2 h per day at 17°C for 6 weeks significantly increased the metabolic activity of brown adipose tissue, leading to a decline in body fat [].

The significant weight loss not observed in ND+MSE condition may be attributed to two possibilities. First, in nonobese mice, the baseline body fat is low, making it difficult to observe
weight-reduction effects in the ND+MSE group compared with the ND group. Weight loss effects are more easily observed in obese conditions; however, the difference becomes smaller or harder to
detect in lean subjects. For example, the fat-suppressing effect of UCP1 is more noticeable in subjects with higher amounts of body fat []. Second, HFD
often activates brown adipose tissue (e.g., increased UCP1 expression), which is believed to be related to the activation of the sympathetic nervous system because of food intake [,]. Therefore, the brown adipose tissue activation and body fat reduction effects of MSE may act synergistically
with the effects of HFD. This is reasonable because in lean conditions, excessive catabolism is prevented, while in the obese condition, body fat is effectively reduced. In humans, the body
fat reduction effect of food components that promote thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue negatively correlates with initial visceral fat levels [].

Finally, the possible underlying mechanism may be the amelioration of deteriorated sleep stability caused by HFD-induced obesity. Guan[] established HFD-induced obesity in mice by feeding them with HFD for 6 weeks, confirming the increased prevalence of NREM sleep and wakefulness but not REM sleep episodes.
Subsequently, they switched the diet to ND for 4 weeks and observed that the obesity-induced increase in NREM sleep and wakefulness frequency was reversible with weight loss because of reduced
energy intake. In the present study, we found that HFD-induced obesity was completely suppressed by the addition of 1% MSE, indicating a synergistic effect between the anti-obesity properties
of MSE and the restoration of sleep-wake parameters. We also found that, both NREM sleep and wake episodes in the HFD+MSE group were significantly lower than those of the HFD group, returning
to levels comparable to those of the ND group. The average length of NREM sleep and wake episodes also significantly increased, to eventually reach ND group levels. The histogram patterns of
sleep-wake episode lengths essentially returned to those of ND levels, indicating that sleep architecture was almost completely restored through MSE supplementation. This restoration can be
attributed to the anti-obesity effects of MSE, which were likely to enhance hormonal balance, including cytokines and adipokines, and the function of the autonomic nervous system, thereby
alleviating sleep fragmentation in conjunction with the amelioration of metabolic syndrome. Another possibility is that, since MSE also possesses central cognitive and memory effects, it may
directly exert an influence on the sleep-wake system. In HFD-induced obese mice, the mRNA expression of the prepro-orexin gene, which serves as an indicator of the activity state of orexin
neurons crucial in sleep–wake regulation, decreased []. Investigating whether MSE restores this hypothalamic neuropeptide expression may elucidate the
neural mechanisms underlying the improvement of sleep stability by MSE supplementation.
articles.abstract:
Dietary supplementation with melinjo (L.) seed extract (MSE) has been an integral part of an anti-obesity therapeutic regimen. To examine the relationship
between anti-obesity and sleep, we explored the effect of MSE on sleep structure in high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obese mice. Although HFD did not alter the total amount of daily sleep, it
significantly reduced the average duration of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and wakefulness episodes and significantly increased the number of these episodes. These findings indicate
fragmented NREM sleep due to repeated brief awakenings in the HFD-fed mice. When 1% (w/v) MSE was given to HFD-fed mice, their weight or sleep structure were comparable to those of ND-fed
mice, proving that dietary MSE completely hindered HFD-induced weight gain and sleep/wake fragmentation. Our data provide compelling evidence that MSE is a novel and promising dietary

articles.title: Melinjo-derived Gnetin C restores metabolic balancedual adipose and hepatic effects in high-fat diet mice
articles.full_text:
Introduction

Type 2 diabetes, which accounts for roughly 90% of diabetes cases, arises from a combination of genetic predisposition and lifestyle factors such as poor diet and insufficient exercise. As a chronic condition, diabetes demands both effective prevention strategies and mitigation of severe complications, including neuropathy, retinopathy, and nephropathy, which can significantly impact patients’ quality of life and healthcare systems. The global increase in body mass index (BMI) underscores obesity as a critical risk factor for diabetes. Although current therapies exist, their limited efficacy, elevated cost, and potential adverse effects often confine their use to the most severe cases, highlighting an urgent need for more effective and broadly accessible interventions. Against this backdrop, the search for novel agents derived from natural products has gained momentum, driven by the unique biochemical mechanisms and favorable safety profiles that such compounds often exhibit.

Resveratrol, a polyphenol in grape skins, has attracted substantial interest because of its anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-aging properties, and has been investigated in a range of disease contexts. Several studies have documented Resveratrol’s positive effects on obesity and diabetes in high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice. In particular, resveratrol promotes the expression of disulfide bond A oxidoreductase-like protein (DsbA-L) in adipocytes, thereby enhancing the multimerization of adiponectin (APN), a process that alleviates metabolic dysfunction. However, its rapid metabolism and low bioavailability present major obstacles to clinical application. Consequently, Gnetin C, a-resveratrol dimer demonstrating greater in vivo stability, emerged as a promising alternative.

Gnetin C is abundant in the seeds of Melinjo (), a Southeast Asian plant often referred to locally as the “Tree of Life.” Melinjo seed extract (MSE) reportedly confers various health benefits, including anti-cancer, anti-periodontitis, anti-bacterial and anti-diabetic effects, and has demonstrated high safety margins in toxicological evaluations (LD₅₀ > 5,000 mg/kg; NOAEL = 1,000 mg/kg). Prior work showed that oral MSE administration improves obesity and diabetes in HFD-fed mice through mechanisms involving DsbA-L and APN, yet the key active component and its precise pharmacological mechanisms remain unclear.

Multi-organ regulation underlies metabolic health, especially in the context of adipose-liver dysfunction during obesity. MSE influences both of these organs and was previously identified as a promising modulator of metabolic disorders, yet its active constituent was unknown. Gnetin C, a-resveratrol dimer found in MSE, likely fulfills that role, but its direct metabolic function remains to be clarified. Consistently, our recent work suggests that Gnetin C ameliorates non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in a manner similar to MSE, implicating this compound as the prime candidate behind MSE’s multi-organ regulatory potential. These observations are especially relevant given the complex interplay between adipose tissue and the liver in obesity-driven metabolic dysfunction, underscoring the importance of a multi-tissue therapeutic strategy. By leveraging the distinct properties of natural products, as demonstrated by Gnetin C, we can explore new prophylactic and therapeutic approaches for obesity and diabetes.

Therefore, in this study, we administered oral Gnetin C to HFD-fed mice to determine whether this dimer functions as the principal active component of MSE, specifically through its regulation of both adipose tissue and the liver. Additionally, we aimed to elucidate its distinctive mode of action against obesity and diabetes. By uncovering the novel mechanisms of Gnetin C, we seek to highlight the broader potential of natural product-derived compounds in advancing both prophylactic and therapeutic strategies for metabolic disorders.

Results

Gnetin C improves body weight and fasting blood glucose level in HFD-fed mice

Gnetin C, a resveratrol-like compound found in MSE and one of its key components, has previously been reported to exert beneficial effects on NAFLD. Therefore, in this study, we investigated whether Gnetin C could improve the pathological conditions of an HFD-induced obesity and diabetes model, similar to MSE. To induce obesity and diabetes, 4-week-old C57BL/6J mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD)for 10 weeks. Starting from week 6 of HFD feeding, Gnetin C (100 or 200 mg/kg) and MSE (1,000 mg/kg) were administered daily by oral gavage for 4 weeks (Fig.a). Body weight and fasting blood glucose levels were measured over time to evaluate the effects of Gnetin C and MSE. Both the Gnetin C- and MSE-treated groups showed reductions in body weight (Fig.b, c). Notably, Gnetin C at 100 mg/kg exerted weight loss comparable to MSE at 1,000 mg/kg, while Gnetin C at 200 mg/kg led to even greater weight reduction. In contrast, administration of Gnetin C at 200 mg/kg in wild-type mice did not produce the same stable weight reduction seen in the model mice—that is, no weight loss was observed under normal conditions—suggesting that the weight loss induced by Gnetin C is attributable to its alleviation of metabolic toxicity under high‐fat diet challenge (Supplementary Fig. 1). Similarly, fasting blood glucose levels were normalized in both Gnetin C- and MSE-treated groups (Fig.d, e). To assess the impact of Gnetin C and MSE on systemic oxidative stress induced by obesity and diabetes, levels of oxidative stress marker d-ROMs and antioxidant capacity (BAP) were measured in serum. Both Gnetin C and MSE significantly reduced oxidative stress and enhanced antioxidant capacity (Fig.f, g). These findings indicate that Gnetin C exerts anti-obesity and anti-diabetic effects similar to those of MSE, suggesting that Gnetin C is the key active component of MSE.

Gnetin C reduces fat accumulation and promotes APN multimerization in adipose tissue

To evaluate the effects of Gnetin C and MSE on fat accumulation, subcutaneous and epididymal fat were excised at the time of dissection, and their weights were measured. Both Gnetin C- and MSE-treated groups exhibited reduced subcutaneous and epididymal fat mass (Fig.a-c). Although Gnetin C conferred metabolic improvements similar to MSE, it remains unclear whether their mechanisms of action are identical. To assess the effects of Gnetin C and MSE on circulating APN and high-molecular-weight (HMW) APN levels, ELISA was performed using mouse serum. Because APN is secreted from adipocytes, the ELISA data were normalized to fat mass. Both Gnetin C and MSE increased total APN levels, and notably, Gnetin C significantly elevated HMW APN levels (Fig.d, e); moreover, the extent of this increase was more pronounced than that of LMW APN (total APN minus HMW APN) (Fig.f), suggesting that APN multimerization plays a crucial role in the metabolic improvements conferred by Gnetin C.

Further analysis revealed that Gnetin C did not alter the expression of endoplasmic reticulum protein 44 (Erp44), another factor involved in APN multimerization, in adipose tissue. However, Gnetin C significantly increased the expression of DsbA-L and endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductase 1α (Ero-1α), both key factors that promote APN multimerization (Fig.g, Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Additionally, Gnetin C enhanced the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), a known upstream regulator of DsbA-L and Ero-1α (Fig.h-j, Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). These findings suggest that Gnetin C promotes APN multimerization and exerts metabolic benefits by activating the PPARγ-DsbA-L-Ero-1α axis. Beyond these multimerization-related factors, we also assessed a panel of genes related to lipid metabolism. In adipose tissue, Gnetin C increased the expression of genes associated with fatty acid synthesis, adipocyte differentiation, lipolysis, and fatty acid β-oxidation (Fig.j).

Gnetin C increases FGF21 expression by activating the upstream regulator Sirt1

To evaluate the effects of Gnetin C on hepatic lipid accumulation, H&E staining was performed. The results showed that Gnetin C reduced lipid accumulation in the liver (Fig.a, b). In addition, liver weight was not significantly affected by Gnetin C treatment (Fig.c). Next, to identify the key regulatory factors underlying the lipid-lowering effects of Gnetin C in the liver, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of genes involved in fatty acid synthesis, triglyceride synthesis, fatty acid β-oxidation, and oxidative stress. Among these genes, fibroblast growth factor 21 (Fgf21), which is associated with fatty acid β-oxidation, was significantly upregulated (Fig.d). FGF21, a hepatocyte secreted by the liver, is known for its potent metabolic regulatory effects on adipose tissue and other organs, making it a subject of intense research. Measurement of circulating FGF21 levels by ELISA, normalized to liver weight, revealed that Gnetin C further enhanced the HFD-induced increase in FGF21 secretion (Fig.e). Considering that obesity is associated with increased FGF21 secretion and FGF21 resistance, the additional upregulation of endogenous FGF21 may be crucial for the metabolic improvements observed in Gnetin C treatment.

However, immunohistochemical analysis of PPARα in liver tissue showed that Gnetin C did not alter PPARα expression (Fig.f, g). We then turned our attention to sirtuin 1 (Sirt1), a NAD-dependent protein deacetylase known to induce FGF21 expression and improve fatty liver. Previous studies have shown that resveratrol, a Sirt1 activator, enhances AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation and mitochondrial function in a Sirt1-dependent manner. Given that Gnetin C is a resveratrol dimer, we hypothesized that Gnetin C might similarly influence Sirt1 expression. Immunohistochemical analysis of Sirt1 in liver tissue revealed that Gnetin C increased Sirt1 expression (Fig.h, i), suggesting that Sirt1 upregulation may contribute to the increase in FGF21 expression observed with Gnetin C treatment.

Gnetin C suppresses fat accumulation in adipose and hepatic cells in vitro

It remains unclear whether the effects of Gnetin C on adipose and liver tissues are direct or mediated indirectly through APN or FGF21. To clarify this, we investigated the direct effects of Gnetin C in vitro. First, we used differentiated adipocytes derived from mouse 3T3-L1 preadipocyte. After 10 days of differentiation, 3T3-L1 adipocytes were treated with Gnetin C. Gnetin C not only reduced lipid accumulation (Fig.a, b), but it also produced a profile similar to the in vivo results: a slight increase in LMW APN levels in the culture supernatant, but a marked increase in HMW APN (Fig.c-e). These findings suggest that Gnetin C directly promotes APN multimerization in adipose tissue, thereby suppressing lipid accumulation.

Next, we used HepG2 cells, a human hepatoma-derived cell line treated with the saturated fatty acid palmitic acid to induce lipid accumulation. Similar to 3T3-L1 adipocytes, Gnetin C treatment reduced lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells (Fig.f and g). Moreover, the expression of Fgf21 and Sirt1 was upregulated (Fig.h-j, Supplementary Fig. 4a, b), suggesting that Gnetin C directly activates the Sirt1-FGF21 axis in liver tissue to suppress lipid accumulation.

Gnetin C enhances hepatic SIRT1 activity and directly activates SIRT1 in vitro

Previous studies have reported that resveratrol enhances Sirt1 activity by directly binding to it. To investigate whether Gnetin C enhances Sirt1 activity through similar mechanisms, a Sirt1 activity assay was performed. This assay measures fluorescence emitted by acetylated substrates upon their deacetylation by Sirt1 in the presence of NAD⁺ and tissue or cell lysates (Fig.a). When liver lysates from Fig.were tested, Sirt1 activity was found to be increased in the Gnetin C-treated group (Fig.b). Similarly, Sirt1 activity was elevated in lysates from HepG2 cells treated with Gnetin C (Fig.c), consistent with the increase in Sirt1 expression (Fig.i, j). These findings indicate that Gnetin C enhances Sirt1 activity in vivo, particularly in liver tissue. Next, to determine whether Gnetin C enhances Sirt1 activity through a direct binding mechanism, a Sirt1 activator screening assay was performed. This assay evaluates direct activation by incubating acetylated substrates and NAD⁺ with candidate direct activators in the presence of recombinant Sirt1 protein (Fig.d). As a positive control, the extent of Sirt1 activation by resveratrol was compared with a negative control (0.1% DMSO). Consistent with previous reports, resveratrol exhibited a concentration-dependent direct activation of Sirt1 (Fig.e). When tested under the same condition, Gnetin C also demonstrated a concentration-dependent direct activation of Sirt1, similar to resveratrol. Notably, under these conditions, Gnetin C induced a higher level of Sirt1 activation than resveratrol (Fig.f), indicating that Gnetin C can directly activate Sirt1 in vitro and may exhibit stronger activity than resveratrol in this context.

Gnetin C enhances expression of FGF21 receptors in hepatocytes and adipocytes: implications for autocrine and paracrine effects

Previous studies have reported that FGF21 suppresses hepatic lipid accumulation through autocrine action, and it exerts paracrine effects on various organs. Among these paracrine effects, its impact on adipose tissue is particularly significant, as FGF21 has been shown to increase APN levels in adipose tissue, thereby improving glucose and lipid metabolism. Additionally, FGF21 has been reported to activate the PPARγ-DsbA-L-Ero-1α pathwayand increase HMW APN levels. These findings suggest that Gnetin C may exert its effects not only through direct action on adipose tissue but also by enhancing the paracrine effects of FGF21, promoting APN multimerization in adipose tissue. To investigate the potential role of FGF21-mediated autocrine and paracrine signaling in the metabolic improvements induced by Gnetin C, we analyzed the expression of FGF21 receptors in adipose and liver tissues. FGF21 receptors consist of a cell surface receptor complex comprising fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) and the co-receptor protein βKlotho, and the expression levels of both components were examined. In liver tissue, Gnetin C increased FGFR1 expression but did not affect βKlotho expression (Fig.a, b). These findings, together with the results in Fig., suggest that FGF21 upregulated by Gnetin C contributes to the suppression of hepatic lipid accumulation primarily through autocrine action. In adipose tissue, Gnetin C increased βKlotho expression but did not alter FGFR1 expression (Fig.c, d). This observation suggests that, in addition to Gnetin C’s dual adipose and hepatic actions, FGF21 upregulated by Gnetin C may act on adipose tissueparacrine signaling, activating the PPARγ-DsbA-L-Ero-1α axis and thereby partially contributing to APN multimerization (Fig.e).

Discussion

In our previous work, we found that MSE alleviates obesity-related metabolic disorders by promoting APN multimerization. To identify the active component responsible for this effect, we focused on Gnetin C, a principal compound found in MSE. Here, we demonstrate that Gnetin C exerts anti-obesity and anti-diabetic effects similar to MSE, primarily by enhancing APN multimerization through DsbA-L upregulation in adipose tissue, consistent with the action of MSE. Moreover, our results showed that Gnetin C also increases the expression of Ero-1α, another critical factor for APN multimerization. Like DsbA-L, Ero-1α catalyzes disulfide bond formation in APN, facilitating its secretion from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Conversely, Erp44, whose expression remained unchanged, plays an essential role in the quality control of APN by binding to APN to form LMW APN and then dissociating upon disulfide bond formation with Ero-1α, thereby enabling the formation of HMW APN. These findings suggest that Gnetin C predominantly influences HMW APN formation by regulating APN’s high-order multimerization factors rather than contributing to LMW APN formation. In addition, we investigated PPARγ, an upstream regulator of these APN multimerization factors. Although PPARγ is known to regulate the expression of DsbA-L, Ero-1α, and Erp44, our results imply that additional upstream regulators may be involved in the Gnetin C-mediated upregulation of DsbA-L and Ero-1α, necessitating further study.

In addition to multimerization-related factors, the gene expression analysis revealed that Gnetin C increased the expression of several genes involved in lipid metabolism in adipose tissue. Some of these, such as Slc2a4 (GLUT4) and G0s2, are recognized downstream targets of PPARγ, consistent with the observed activation of the PPARγ-DsbA-L-Ero-1α axis. The induction of Acaca and Chrebp, both lipogenic genes, likely reflects activation oflipogenesis programs during adipocyte differentiation. Given that GLUT4 is a known PPARγ target and can regulate Chrebp activity, and that Chrebp directly controls Acaca expression, these changes may represent downstream consequences of PPARγ activation that also contribute to systemic insulin sensitivity. In parallel, Irf4 and its downstream coactivator Pgc1α, together with Pparα and its target gene Acox1, were also upregulated, pointing to enhanced lipolysis, mitochondrial biogenesis, and fatty acid oxidation. These findings suggest that Gnetin C may influence adipose metabolism not only through PPARγ-dependent pathways but alsoadditional transcriptional programs.

We also demonstrated that Gnetin C ameliorates obesity and diabetes partly by increasing FGF21 expression and secretion in the liver. FGF21 functions as a hepatocyte with both autocrine and paracrine effects. However, to clarify the contributions of these mechanisms, further work using tissue-specific FGF21 receptor-deficient models is required. While our study focused on adipose tissue, the most reported target of FGF21’s paracrine effects, FGF21 also promotes β-cell proliferation and function in the pancreas, improves insulin sensitivity in muscle, and activates sympathetic nerves through the hypothalamus, suggesting additional organ-level contributions to the improvements in obesity and diabetes mediated by Gnetin C. Furthermore, although we confirmed the upregulation and activation of Sirt1, an upstream regulator of FGF21, other factors such as PPARα, activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 α (PGC-1α)may also play roles and warrant further investigation.

Although the precise molecular mechanisms underlying the SIRT1-mediated regulation of FGF21 were not directly addressed in this study, previous reports provide important insights. For example, SIRT1 has been shown to regulate FGF21 expression in the liver, and more recently, the metabolic benefits of resveratrol have been reported to depend on FGF21 signaling. These findings indicate that the SIRT1-FGF21 regulatory axis is increasingly recognized as a key pathway in metabolic regulation. Our present data support this concept by demonstrating Gnetin C-induced activation of SIRT1 accompanied by FGF21 upregulation. Nevertheless, the mechanistic basis of this regulation remains unclear. Future studies incorporating chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays and analyses of histone acetylation at the FGF21 promoter will be crucial for determining whether SIRT1 directly regulates FGF21 transcriptionchromatin remodeling. Moreover, the direct causal relationships among Gnetin C, SIRT1 activation, FGF21 induction, and APN multimerization remain to be established and should be confirmed in additional mechanistic studies.

Our previous work has shown that Gnetin C improves blood lipid profiles, including significant reductions in plasma triglyceride and total cholesterol levels, and attenuates hepatic lipid accumulation in an NAFLD mouse model. In addition, that study showed suppression of hepatic genes related to triglyceride synthesis and transport (e.g., Dgat1, Dgat2, Mtp). Importantly, our data (Fig.d) likewise demonstrate a significant downregulation of Dgat2 expression in the liver, which is consistent with the reported mechanism of Gnetin C. Together, these convergent findings strengthen the notion that Gnetin C contributes to the lipid-lowering effects of MSE through suppression of triglyceride synthesis and improvement of systemic lipid metabolism.

Despite ongoing debate regarding the direct activation of Sirt1 by resveratrol, our Sirt1 activator screening assay confirmed its concentration-dependent activation, in agreement with previous studies. Notably, we demonstrated for the first time that Gnetin C, a resveratrol dimer, exhibits stronger activity than resveratrol in our in vitro assay, supporting its potential as a SIRT1 activator. Importantly, the comparison between resveratrol and Gnetin C in this study was made using a recombinant SIRT1-based screening assay (Fig.d-f), which directly assesses the intrinsic ability of compounds to activate SIRT1 and is not influenced by pharmacokinetic properties. Thus, the stronger activation observed for Gnetin C reflects a direct molecular effect. Furthermore, prior reports have shown greater in vivo retention of Gnetin C and superior improvements in body weight, liver weight, and insulin sensitivity relative to resveratrol in a NAFLD model. These findings complement our in vitro data and collectively support Gnetin C as a promising activator of SIRT1. Additional assessments beyond the screening assay remain necessary to fully validate these findings.

Our results suggest that Gnetin C may promote APN multimerization not only through activation of the PPARγ-DsbA-L-Ero-1α axis in adipose tissue but also indirectlythe Sirt1-FGF21 axis in the liver, highlighting its promise as a novel agent for metabolic disease therapy. Although Gnetin C shows promise for improving NAFLDand potentially mitigating periodontal disease through antioxidant effects, preventing Alzheimer’s disease, and exerting anti-inflammatory actions, these findings remain limited and require further investigation. Gnetin C also exhibits potent antioxidant properties, contributing to pronounced anti-cancer effects, underscoring its broader clinical relevance. However, our data reveal that high-dose Gnetin C administration can induce gastrointestinal symptoms in mice, such as diarrhea and lymphangiectasia-like conditions (described in the Methods section). Given that Gnetin C is known to have strong bioactivity (including anticancer properties), there are legitimate safety concerns at elevated concentrations, necessitating cautious evaluation. The small sample size of the high-dose group constitutes a limitation of the present study, and further investigations are warranted to validate the safety profile of Gnetin C.

In contrast, MSE demonstrates stable efficacy with fewer gastrointestinal side effects. Consistent with previous safety assessments, our current results confirm that MSE exhibits a robust safety profile, distinctly different from the adverse effects observed with high-dose Gnetin C administration. Intriguingly, our recent study showed that MSE administration leads to high circulating levels of Gnetin C and its glycosylated derivatives, including Gnemonoside A. This finding prompts further exploration into whether non-Gnetin C components, or particularly Gnetin C glycosides, contribute to MSE’s overall therapeutic effects. In any case, both MSE and Gnetin C exert beneficial actions through direct impact on the liver and adipose tissue and through inter-organ mechanisms involving the liver-adipose axis. These insights offer valuable information for developing multi-target treatment strategies against metabolic disorders.

Methods

Materials and chemicals

MSE powder (YMP-M-181201), containing 0.07% RES, 2.41% gnetin C, 23.9% gnemonoside A, 4.51% gnemonoside D, and 9% dextrin as an excipient, was obtained from the Yamada Bee Company, Inc. (Okayama, Japan). Gnetin C (purity: >98%, HPLC) was prepared according to a previously described method.

Experimental animals and treatments

C57BL/6J mice were housed in the animal experimentation facility at Kumamoto University in accordance with the guidelines of the university’s Animal Facility Center. The mice were maintained under a 12-hour light/dark cycle at a room temperature of 20 °C. For HFD, we purchased the chow from Oriental Yeast Co., Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan), and replaced once weekly with 300 g of fresh chow after an overnight fasting period. The composition of the HFD was 25% casein, 20% safflower oil, 14% beef tallow, 8% dextrin, 7% lactose, 7% sucrose, and 5% cellulose. Five-week-old mice were randomly divided into five groups and fed with the HFD for six weeks. After ensuring that the average body weight of each group was similar at the end of the sixth week, the mice were fed HFD for an additional four weeks. MSE was administered once daily for four weeks at a dose of 1,000 mg/kg by oral gavage using a gastric tube. Similarly, Gnetin C was administered once daily for four weeks at doses of 100 mg/kg or 200 mg/kg by oral gavage using a gastric tube. The Gnetin C dose was determined based on the amount of Gnetin C and its glycosides present in 1,000 mg/kg of MSE. Notably, 1,000 mg/kg of MSE contains not only Gnetin C but also its glycosides (Gnemonosides), and assuming complete conversion of these glycosides to Gnetin C, while also accounting for inter-lot variations, the effective dose is estimated to fall within the range of 100 to 200 mg/kg. Therefore, two dose levels of 100 and 200 mg/kg were established. In the high-concentration group (200 mg/kg), gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and lymphangiectasia-like conditions were frequently observed in mice. Before administration, the test compounds were thoroughly suspended using a mortar and pestle.　Blood glucose levels were measured using an Accu-Chek Compact glucometer (Roche, Basel, Switzerland), with blood samples collectedtail vein puncture. Fasting blood glucose levels were measured after more than 12 h of fasting, during which water was freely available. Anesthesia was induced in mice using an intraperitoneal injection of three types of mixed anesthesia (0.75 mg/kg of medetomidine [NIPPON ZENYAKU KOGYO CO., LTD., Fukushima, Japan], 4 mg/kg of midazolam [Sandoz K. K., Tokyo, Japan] and 5 mg/kg of butorphanol [Meiji Animal Health Co., Ltd., Kumamoto, Japan]). Following confirmation of a surgical plane of anesthesia, euthanasia was performed by exsanguination via cardiac puncture. These procedures adhered to the 2020 AVMA Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals. The animal study was conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines (Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments). All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Welfare Committee of Kumamoto University (#A2024-050, to T.S.) and conducted in compliance with the relevant national and institutional guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.

Cell culture

3T3-L1 cells (RIKEN BRC, Japan) were used to evaluate the direct effects of Gnetin C on adipocytes. The cells were cultured in DMEM (High Glucose) medium (Wako, Osaka, Japan) supplemented with 10% Fetal Calf Serum (FCS) and 1% antibiotics (P/S; Penicillin G [100 U/mL] and Streptomycin [100 µg/mL]). To induce differentiation, the cells were maintained at confluence for two days, then the medium was replaced with 3T3-L1 adipocyte differentiation medium (KAC, Kyoto, Japan) and cultured for three days. Subsequently, the cells were cultured in a 3T3-L1 adipocyte culture medium (KAC, Kyoto, Japan) for seven days. HepG2 cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and used to evaluate the direct effects of Gnetin C on hepatocytes. The cells were cultured in DMEM (Low Glucose) medium (Wako, Osaka, Japan) supplemented with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) and 1% antibiotics (P/S; Penicillin G [100 U/mL] and Streptomycin [100 µg/mL]). To induce lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells, the cells were treated with 0.3 mM palmitic acid (Thermo Fisher, Massachusetts, USA) for 18 h. For maintenance culture, the culture dishes (3003 dishes, Falcon, Texas, USA) were pre-coated with Cell Matrix type I-C (Nitta Gelatin, Osaka, Japan) and incubated at 37 °C for at least 30 min before use. All cells were cultured in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO₂.

Total RNA was extracted from mouse adipose and liver tissues, 3T3-L1 cells, and HepG2 cells using RNAiso Plus. The reactions were carried out using a CFX Connect™ Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, California, USA). Protein isolation and western blotting

Proteins were extracted from mouse adipose tissue and HepG2 cells using RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.5], 150 mM NaCl, 1 mg/mL sodium deoxycholate, 1 mM Na₃VO₄, and 1% protease inhibitor cocktail). Protein concentrations were measured using the BCA method. Next, proteins were separated on 8% or 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to a PVDF membrane (250 mA, 1.5 h). The membrane was then blocked for 1 h with 0.05% PBS-Tween containing 5% skim milk. After washing in 0.05% PBS-Tween, the membrane was incubated at room temperature for 1 h with primary antibodies diluted in Can Get SignalSolution 1 (TOYOBO, Osaka, Japan). Following the primary antibody incubation, the membrane was washed with 0.05% PBS-Tween and incubated at room temperature for 1 h with secondary antibodies diluted in Can Get SignalSolution 2 (TOYOBO, Osaka, Japan). After this incubation, the membrane was washed with 0.05% PBS-Tween, treated with Super SignalWest Pico chemiluminescent substrate (Thermo Fisher, Massachusetts, USA), and signals were detected using the Vilber Bio Imaging Fusion system (Vilber Lourmat, Collégien, France). The detected bands were quantified using ImageJ software. Primary antibodies used were anti-PPARγ (sc-7273, Santa Cruz, Texas, USA) and anti-Sirt1 (sc-15404, Santa Cruz, Texas, USA). Anti-Hsc70 (ADI-SPA-815, Enzo Life Sciences, New York, USA) and anti-vinculin (sc-73614, Santa Cruz, Texas, USA) were used as loading controls.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

Serum levels of total APN and HMW-APN were quantified using a Mouse HMW & Total APN ELISA kit (ALPCO, New Hampshire, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Similarly, FGF21 levels were measured using a Mouse/Rat FGF21 ELISA kit (R&D Systems, Minnesota, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. For these measurements, serum was obtained by centrifuging blood collected from the inferior vena cava of mice at 5,000 rpm and 4 °C for 30 min. Cell culture supernatants were also used for the assays.

d-ROMs and BAP test

Plasma levels of diacron-Reactive Oxygen Metabolites (d-ROMs) and Biological Antioxidant Potential (BAP) were measured using the Free Carrio Duo system (WISMERLL, Tokyo, Japan) and the corresponding d-ROMs and BAP test kits (WISMERLL, Tokyo, Japan), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For sample preparation, serum was obtained by centrifuging blood collected from the inferior vena cava of mice at 5,000 rpm and 4 °C for 30 min.

Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) staining and quantification

Mouse livers were excised, washed with PBS (-), and immersed in 10% neutral buffered formalin at room temperature for 12 h. Following formalin fixation, the tissues were washed three times with PBS (-) and dehydrated with ethanol. Subsequent steps, including paraffin embedding and H&E staining, were outsourced to K.I. Steiner (Kumamoto, Japan). Stained images were captured using a BZ-X710 microscope (Keyence, Osaka, Japan), and lipid droplet quantification was performed using ImageJ software.

Oil red O staining and quantification

After removing the culture medium from HepG2 and 3T3-L1 cells, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, then washed and dehydrated with 60% isopropanol. Subsequently, the cells were treated with a Oil red O staining solution and incubated in the dark for 20 min. After removing the staining solution, Milli-Q (MQ) water was added, and stained images were captured using a BZ-X710 microscope (Keyence, Osaka, Japan). ImageJ software was used for further analysis and quantification of the stained images.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining

Paraffin-embedded liver tissue sections prepared for IHC staining were deparaffinized and immersed in Target Retrieval Solution (DAKO, Glostrup, Denmark). Antigen retrieval was performed using an autoclave at 121 °C for 20 min. To prevent non-specific staining, the VECTOR M.O.M. Immunodetection kit (VEC, California, USA) was used. The sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C in the dark with a 1:100 dilution of an anti-PPARα antibody (sc-398394, Santa Cruz, Texas, USA) and an anti-Sirt1 antibody (sc-15404, Santa Cruz, Texas, USA). On the following day, the sections were treated with M.O.M. Biotinylated Anti-Mouse IgG Reagent (VEC, California, USA), and the reaction was visualized using a diaminobenzidine (DAB) substrate system (Nichirei, Tokyo, Japan). Stained images were acquired using a Nano Zoomer S20 Digital Slide Scanner (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan), and the number of PPARαand Sirt1cells was quantified using HALO software (Indica Labs, Corrales, USA).

Quantification of Sirt1 activity assay and Sirt1 activator screening assay

SIRT1 activity was assessed using a fluorogenic peptide substrate bearing an N-terminal fluorophore and a C-terminal quencher. Upon deacetylation by active SIRT1 in the presence of NAD⁺, the concurrently supplied protease (Developer) cleaves the substrate, separating the quencher from the fluorophore and generating fluorescence, thereby enabling quantification of deacetylase activity. For the SIRT1 activity assay, MQ water and kit components (SIRT1 Assay Buffer, Fluoro-Substrate Peptide, NAD⁺, and Developer) were added to microtiter plate wells, followed by the addition of liver tissue and HepG2 cell lysates, and the plate was incubated at room temperature. Fluorescence was measured 60 min after lysate addition at Ex/Em = 350/460 nm using a BioTek Cytation 5 plate reader (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA). This protocol quantifies NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase activity present in lysates and thus reports SIRT1 activity.

For the SIRT1 activator screening assay, MQ water and kit reagents (SIRT1 Assay Buffer, Fluoro-Substrate Peptide, and NAD⁺) were dispensed into microtiter wells. Resveratrol (LKT Laboratories, MN, USA) and Gnetin C, prepared as previously described, were applied at 10 − 1,000 µM (each in 0.1% DMSO) or vehicle control (0.1% DMSO), after which Developer and recombinant SIRT1 were added, and the reaction was incubated at room temperature. Fluorescence was measured 10 min after enzyme addition at Ex/Em = 350/460 nm using a BioTek Cytation 5 plate reader. This protocol measures the direct effects of test compounds on recombinant SIRT1 deacetylase activity under defined, NAD⁺-dependent conditions; increases in fluorescence indicate activation, whereas decreases indicate inhibition, independent of cellular signaling contexts.

Statistical analysis

Experimental data are presented as the mean ± SEM. Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s post-hoc test, with a significance level set at< 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software, California, USA).

articles.abstract:
Multi-organ regulation underlies metabolic health, especially in the context of adipose-liver dysfunction during obesity. Previous findings identified Melinjo seed extract (MSE) as a promising modulator of metabolic disorders, although its active component remained unknown. Gnetin C, a-resveratrol dimer from MSE, likely serves as the key factor, yet its direct metabolic role remains unclear. Here, Gnetin C was administered to high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, which significantly improved body weight and fasting glucose, attributed to enhanced adiponectin (APN) multimerization. In adipose tissue, Gnetin C directly promotes APN multimerization and suppresses fat accumulation by up-regulating the PPARγ-DsbA-L axis, while concurrently modulating hepatic Sirt1, which may contribute to increased FGF21 production. This paracrine FGF21 signaling, suggested by elevated Fgfr1 in hepatocytes and βKlotho in adipocytes, further augments APN multimerization. These findings underscore the importance of a multi-tissue approach to obesity management and position Gnetin C as an integrative therapeutic candidate, restoring metabolic balancedual adipose and hepatic effects in HFD mice.

articles.title: Antitumor activity of melinjo (L.) seed extract in human and murine tumor models in vitro and in a colon-26 tumor-bearing mouse model in vivo
articles.full_text:
Introduction

Melinjo (L.), a member of the Gnetaceae family, is an arboreal dioecious plant widely cultivated in Southeast Asia. Its fruits, seeds, leaves, and flowers are edible,. Melinjo seeds have a high nutritive value, and are consumed as a major food item by the Indonesian population. The melinjo seeds are rich in dimeric stilbenoids, such as gnetin C (GC) and its glucosides (gnemonosides A, C, and D), with-piceid glucoside as a minor constituent, including negligible amount (0.1%) of-resveratrol (RV)–(Fig.). Melinjo seed extract (MSE) is sold as a nutritional supplement in Japan, and is now being introduced into the United States.

Recent studies indicate that the oral administration of MSE is well tolerated and efficiently absorbed, and does not produce significant adverse effects to in laboratory animals or humans. Tatefuji et al.reported that repeated oral administration of MSE (1000 mg/kg per day) in rats had no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL). In addition, a rat bone marrow micronucleus test, which evaluates genotoxicity, was negative for MSE at doses up to 4000 mg/kg per day. Furthermore, a human study conducted in healthy volunteers reported that oral administration of MSE for 28 days, up to an oral dose of 5000 mg, daily, was well tolerated with no observable adverse events.

MSE has been reported to have a broad spectrum of pharmacological effects. For example, an ethanol extract of MSE seeds has antioxidant and radical scavenging activity, similar to that of ascorbic acid and-alpha-tocopherol,. In addition, MSE inhibits the enzymes lipase and alpha-amylase and has antimicrobial activity against food microorganisms and enterobacteria. In mice, MSE produced an antimetabolic syndrome effect by suppressing a gain in body weight and improving insulin resistance. MSE and its active constituents also stimulated the immune response, inhibited angiogenesis, and prevented endothelial senescence. A recent double-blind randomized controlled clinical trial involving healthy adult males demonstrated that administration of 750 mg MSE for 8 weeks reduced serum uric acid levels at 4 and 8 weeks relative to levels in a group dosed with a placebo. It has been reported that MSE may decrease serum uric acid regardless of insulin resistance, and may improve lipid metabolism by increasing levels of HDL cholesterol.

Gnetin C, a dimeric stilbenoid abundant in MSE (Fig.), is reported to have advantages overRV (3,5,4′-trihydoxy--stilbene), a stilbenoid polyphenol in red wine (grape skins). It has been reported that GC may be the most effective component among the MSE derivatives, since it suppressed the angiogenesis-related endothelial cell functions and tumor-induced angiogenesis significantly compared to its glycosides (gnemonosides A, C, and D). Considering the relative amounts of GC, 28.0 mg/g (61.7mol/g), GL, a minor component (4.95mol/g), andRV (5.26mol/g) in MSE, the antiangiogenic effects of MSE have been attributed to GC. While the literature on the effects ofRV on cancer cells is abundant, numerous studies indicate that it has poor bioavailability–. Moreover, the rapid metabolism ofRV is an obstacle to using it in human preclinical studies. In contrast, GC has excellent bioavailability. For example, the concentration of GC was about sixfold higher than that ofRV in streptozotocin-treated and control mice after administration of an ethanol extract ofseeds. In addition, the oral administration of 1000 mg of MSE powder to healthy volunteers indicated that GC was maintained in plasma longer than 96 h, and had a mean residence time (MRT) of 36 h, relative to 24 h forRV, with aof 12 h and an MRT of 14 h. GC inhibits tyrosinase activity, and thus suppresses melanin biosynthesis, in B16 cells. Given the broad spectrum of pharmacological effects reported for MSE and GC, we postulate that MSE and GC have properties that might prevent and/or treat cancer.

Cancer remains the second most common cause of death in the United States, accounting for nearly one of every four deaths. There is an increase in the cancer burden worldwide. Despite decreases in the incidence and mortality rates for most types of cancer (including lung, colorectal, prostate, and female breast cancer) in the United States and many other Western countries, the number of cancer cases and deaths is projected to more than double worldwide over the next 20–40 years,. Notwithstanding the steady progress in drug discovery and effective prevention, the treatment of most cancers remains challenging. The use of several chemotherapeutic drugs, including nontargeted and molecularly targeted agents currently employed in cancer therapy, is severely limited by their adverse side effects. On the other hand, natural compounds that selectively exert cytotoxic effect on cancer cells without affecting normal cells have attracted considerable attention as cancer chemopreventive and cancer therapeutic agents–. Various dietary components found in plant-derived foods have been recognized for their anticarcinogenic properties–. While various plant-derived molecules have shown anticancer properties, only a few with anticancer potential are currently undergoing clinical trials,. Therefore, there is a need to identify plant-derived, bioactive food components with anticancer potential to prevent and/or treat human cancers.

In the present work, we investigated the anticancer potentials of both MSE and its putative active component GC by using various human and murine tumor cell types derived from the pancreas, colon, breast, and prostate for in vitro analysis. Nonmalignant cells were used to determine whether MSE or GC selectively targets cancer cells without affecting normal cells. Since GC is a dimeric stilbenoid (resveratrol dimer derivative),RV was used as a control in the in vitro experiments. Apoptosis assay was performed to determine whether MSE or GC inhibits tumor cell growth by inducing apoptosis. We also performed luminescent caspase-3/7 and caspase-9 assays, to understand whether MSE or GC induces programmed cell death (apoptosis) by activating the caspases. Furthermore, the antitumor efficacy of MSE observed in vitro was also validated in a widely used colon-26 tumor-bearing mouse model. Here, we report that MSE and GC have anticancer potential, and might be useful to prevent and treat certain cancers. Most importantly, we also provide evidence that MSE inhibits tumor growth, angiogenesis, and liver metastasis in a colon-26 tumor-bearing mice model.
